Params: Metal fragments and burning splinters streak past your eyes like a shower of falling stars.
You open your eyes in the real world, standing outside the simulation pod as a sharp pain tears through your head.
It feels like nails being driven slowly into your skull, turning everything inside your mind upside down.
At the final moment, the bridge door jammed.
That tiny delay cost you your chance to escape the blast.
The system severed the sensory connection the moment the impact hit, but the final instant before death—every sense pushed to its limit—still refuses to fade.
A notification chimes. You force your eyes open through gritted teeth and see the number you already expected.
Dying inside the tactical simulation system carries the harshest penalty of all.
You knew what the result would be and can't even bring yourself to care about the score.
All you can think about are the words that unknown woman left you with.
You murmur to the projection screen, the sea wind still howling in your ears.
You remember the figure in red and white, and the certainty in her voice.
She isn't gentle by nature, and she doesn't hide behind pretty words. You could tell that from the way she spoke.

She is a natural leader, someone who belongs on the battlefield, standing proudly in the face of danger. Yet when she spoke those simple words, they brought more than a rush of courage. They left behind a quiet, overwhelming feeling of gratitude and admiration.
Someone had been willing to hold her fire, lower the gangway for strangers, and believe that lives mattered more than winning.
She saw you. She believed in you.
Next time, and every time after that—even on a real battlefield—you'll hold to the same belief.
You return to the main screen and open the post-battle review.
The joy of being understood had briefly kept the pain at bay. Now that you've stopped moving, the shock to your consciousness comes rushing back.
But this is the best time to review the battle, while every detail is still fresh.
Besides, you can still think clearly and move without difficulty. The damage can't be too severe.
When you leave the tactical simulation chamber, the sky beyond F.O.S. is already turning pale with dawn.
Time inside the tactical simulation system doesn't pass at the same rate as it does outside. Even so, remaining connected for that long is unusual.
The pain hasn't faded. It lingers inside your skull like broken shells left on the sand after the tide, impossible to ignore.
At this point, you can't tell whether it's from exhaustion or the simulation itself.
Maybe the relentless wind in the battle had something to do with it too.
Either way, I should go to the medical station first.
Either way, I should get some rest first.
I've also prepared some additional materials on today's topic.
It's been sent to your terminals. Take a look if you'd like to explore it further.
You're welcome to come talk to me if you have any questions. Class dismissed.
The classroom erupts into chatter as soon as the lecture ends.
One point from the lesson stays on your mind, so you open your terminal.
Two new messages from unknown senders are waiting in your inbox.
You checked your messages this morning and there was nothing new, so they must've arrived during class.
You find messages with the same sender in your read folder.
They're the notifications related to the score review and supplemental assessment you requested earlier.
You thought the matter was already settled. Why would the system contact you again now?
"Your tactical simulation assessment score has been updated."
"Your tactical simulation assessment score has been updated."
How could the score be updated? The result of that naval simulation was supposed to be locked the moment you left the pod.
The supplemental assessment score was final and couldn't be changed. The application rules stated that clearly.
You keep reading, but instead of answering your questions, the message only leaves you more confused.
You check the name and student number three times. The report definitely belongs to you.
It isn't only the final number. Every category has been reassessed—tactical decisions, resource allocation, battlefield adaptation—and every comment is completely different from the original report.
The final evaluation is far above the usual range.
You didn't request another review. The interface doesn't even offer that option, let alone a way to submit an appeal.
No one knows what happened during that battle except the person who spoke to you through the storm and cannon fire.
A warmth rises in your chest, strong enough to make you tremble. Suddenly, you want nothing more than to find the white-haired teacher and thank her in person.

A teacher—of course. Her tone, the way she treated you, and the authority to change the system's evaluation all point to the same conclusion. She isn't just a teacher. She's probably a combat instructor.
But even without knowing every rule of the supplemental assessment, you understand that the evaluator's identity is strictly confidential. At least from your side, the test is single-blind.
Combat training won't begin until next semester. Your class has to build a proper foundation in physical techniques before moving on to practical exercises.
Your anticipation for the course only grows.
At the start of the new semester...
There is still some time before class begins, and in the vast training field, the only person waiting is Adelyde, the instructor in charge of the exercise.
The files on the new group of students haven't reached her yet. Not that she needs them.
Student profiles do little more than rank people by their scores, place them in boxes, and attach labels to them.
Adelyde doesn't care whether those numbers are impressive or disappointing. She has never used them to judge a student's ability.
She doesn't trust scores. She trusts what she sees for herself. That was true before the naval simulation, and it's even more true now.

Of course, she knows the system is built around those numbers. She may refuse to use them to sort people into ranks, but she can't pretend they don't affect a student's future. That's why she once chose to change a score.
A distinctive mission alert sounds, and she opens her terminal for a quick look.
For a visiting F.O.S. combat instructor like Adelyde, a full semester of combat training classes is a rare assignment. More often, she spends her days traveling from one mission site to the next.
The new assignment is simple and only requires her presence on-site. Even so, she requests the full briefing and plans to review it after class.
Adelyde submits the request without looking up.
As Adelyde continues working at her terminal, the registering student's information appears on the screen.
She recognizes the string of numbers and looks up at once.
Then she hears your voice. It isn't only the numbers she recognizes.
In that voice, she can almost hear the waves and howling wind again. She can almost smell the salt and gunsmoke.
She wants to see the face behind that voice. She never expects the sight of you to pull her into an even deeper current of emotion.
You stand at the entrance in a standard F.O.S. cadet uniform, your posture straight. You carry the energy of a student, but also a calm beyond your age.
It's like sunlight breaking through storm clouds, a tide washing the shore clean, a lighthouse piercing the fog—and a storm from thirty years ago returning all at once.
You stand at the entrance in a standard F.O.S. cadet uniform, your posture straight. You carry the energy of a student, but also a calm beyond your age.
It's like sunlight breaking through storm clouds, a tide washing the shore clean, a lighthouse piercing the fog—and a storm from thirty years ago returning all at once.
Your face is still a little youthful, still carrying the innocence of your student years.
Even so, the shape of your features already matches the person in her memories. One look at your eyes is enough to make her soul tremble.
The person from the armory. The person from the Atlantic Eye. The person who stood at the bow of that ship.
The person from the armory. The person from the Atlantic Eye. The person who stood at the bow of that ship.
The person she searched for, waited for, and admired had always been the same.
The person she searched for, waited for, and admired had always been the same.
She wants to ask if you're alright, but that's not the kind of thing you say when you've only just met.
No. Not yet. You can't let on that they know each other.
She swallows hard, forcing down a bitterness that has been building for far too long.
...It's a pleasure to meet you. Starting today, I'll be your instructor for this semester.
But it isn't the first time you've met.
She looks at you and sees a voyage that has crossed endless years to reach this moment.
For Adelyde, she has known you for a long time—since the sea burned beneath cannon fire, since the storm at the Atlantic Eye, since all the years filled with waiting and longing.
I'm very glad to meet you.
